My journey started at the University of Windsor, Canada, where I graduated in Computer Science with perfect scores in OOP and Algorithms. During and after my degree, I spent 3+ years at an early-stage SaaS startup called Eatozee, where I worked across the full stack — React.js, Next.js, TypeScript, Node.js, AWS, and MongoDB. I helped scale the platform, cut load times by 60%, grew the user base by 20%, and built systems that handled real production pressure.
Outside of work, I went deep into blockchain — built an open-source NFT toolkit on the XRPL blockchain and got recognized as 1st Runner-Up by the XRPL team for it. That project pushed me into understanding AI-enabled components and decentralized architectures in ways a regular job never would have.
When the startup wound down, I came back to Surat and founded Bhayani Innovations — because I kept seeing the same problem: growing Indian businesses still running on spreadsheets and paper, with no affordable, quality tech partner to help them. We build custom software, automation tools, and mobile apps for them.

**The Problem:**

Enterprise software configuration is prohibitively expensive to automate with AI. At WorkHall, creating business forms with proper fields, validations, and security rules takes 30 minutes manually. When we tried automating this with AI agents to eventually read Business Requirement Documents and auto-generate configurations, we hit a wall: costs of $0.50-$1.00 per field made it economically unfeasible at scale. A typical form with 15 fields would cost $15 in AI automation alone—completely unsustainable for enterprise needs.

**Technical Hurdles:**

The core challenge was that traditional AI agents "think out loud" for every interaction—analyzing screenshots, reasoning about button clicks, verifying results. They burned expensive tokens on repetitive tasks. We needed to fundamentally rethink the approach.

My breakthrough came from capturing network traffic instead of watching UI interactions. I discovered that beneath the complex interface were simple, predictable API patterns. The challenge then became: how do you reverse-engineer undocumented APIs systematically? I developed a progressive learning approach—treating each API error as information rather than failure, iteratively building understanding of the system's contract.

Key technical challenges included:
- Learning complex API structures without documentation
- Managing hierarchical data dependencies (what must be created before what)
- Handling edge cases discovered only through trial
- Building reliable error recovery and retry logic

**Non-Technical Hurdles:**

The bigger challenge was strategic: convincing stakeholders to abandon the "AI does everything" approach for a hybrid model. There was initial resistance to "writing code when we have AI agents." I had to demonstrate through working demos that intelligent division of labor—AI for interpretation, code for execution—wasn't a compromise but a superior architecture.

I also faced the perfectionism trap—wanting to understand the entire system before building anything. Breaking free required embracing incremental progress: ship the simple field types first, learn from real usage, then add complexity.

**How We Succeeded:**

I developed a **Hybrid Code-Agent Architecture** that reduced costs by 95% (from $1.00 to $0.05 per field):

1. **Discovery Phase**: Used AI agents once to explore the UI and capture API patterns (one-time $5-10 investment per workflow type)
2. **Codification**: Automated extraction of API structures from captured traffic
3. **Execution**: Direct API calls via Python scripts—no browser, no screenshots, sub-second execution
4. **Orchestration**: Lightweight AI interprets user intent and calls the right script

**Results:**
- 95% cost reduction ($1.00 → $0.05 per field)
- 60x speed improvement (30 minutes → 30 seconds)
- Currently deployed on AWS EC2 with two Claude Code agents
- Working toward fully autonomous BRD-to-software pipeline

**Key Insight:**

The most important learning wasn't technical—it was strategic: effective AI automation isn't about maximizing AI usage, it's about intelligently dividing labor between AI reasoning (for ambiguity, discovery, interpretation) and deterministic code (for repetitive, validated tasks). This hybrid approach is 20x cheaper, faster, and more reliable than pure AI automation.

This project taught me that production-grade AI systems require economic thinking alongside technical capability. The technically impressive solution isn't always the right one—sustainable AI must balance capability with cost at scale.

My journey began with understanding the raw reality of the Bangladeshi market. Unlike other sectors, ISP marketing happens on the ground. I started by learning the importance of Visibility and Trust. In the early days, my focus was on local branding banners on electric poles, flyers in apartment lobbies, and building relationships with local community influencers.

I learned that in Bangladesh, a customer doesn't just buy "50 Mbps"; they buy the assurance that their kid's online class won't lag and their office files will upload on time. This "ground-level" experience taught me the psychology of the Bangladeshi consumer, which became the foundation of my senior leadership.

Building a Brand, Not Just a Connection
As I moved into a Senior Management role, my objective shifted from Sales to Brand Equity. The ISP market in Bangladesh is highly fragmented and price-sensitive. My biggest contribution was moving the company away from the "Price War."

I realized that if we only compete on price, we lose. Instead, I positioned our service around Reliability and Superior Support. I spearheaded campaigns that focused on "Zero Buffer" lifestyles and "24/7 Human Support." By building a brand identity that stood for quality, I helped the company acquire premium customers who value uptime over the cheapest rate. This strategy significantly increased our Average Revenue Per User (ARPU).

The Art of Retention: Fighting the "Churn"
In the ISP sector, getting a new customer is easy, but keeping them is the real battle. One of my most significant professional achievements has been the implementation of a Customer Retention Framework. I didn't just wait for customers to call and complain. I worked closely with the Technical and Support teams to identify "at-risk" users. By analyzing data, such as frequent connection drops or late bill payments. I designed proactive outreach programs. Whether it was a loyalty discount for long-term users or a "Service Recovery" call after a major fiber cut, these efforts drastically reduced our Churn Rate, ensuring a stable and growing monthly revenue stream for the company.

4. Product Innovation: Segmenting the Market
I recognized early on that a student, a hardcore gamer, and a small business owner have different needs. In my role, I led the launch of Niche-Specific Packages:

The Gamer's Choice: Focusing on low latency and optimized routing for international servers.

The Freelancer Pro: Offering high upload speeds and priority technical support.

SME Bundles: Combining internet with security features for small offices.
This segmentation allowed us to dominate specific market sectors and created a "sticky" customer base that felt the product was made specifically for them.


Managing a marketing department in a top-tier ISP requires balancing the budget with high-octane results. I have led diverse teams—from creative designers to field sales forces—aligning everyone toward a single goal: Market Leadership. I optimized our digital marketing spend by using GEO-targeted ads, ensuring that we only spent money in areas where our fiber footprint was strong. This "Data-First" approach saved the company millions in wasted advertising and improved our Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC).

In the conclusion, my journey is defined by Resilience and Adaptation. In an industry where technology changes every day and competition is fierce, I have proven that a successful Marketing Manager must be part-technician, part-psychologist, and full-time strategist.

I don't just sell "internet"; I sell the bridge that connects millions of Bangladeshis to their dreams, their families, and their global careers. My value lies in my ability to take a technical utility and turn it into a premium, household necessity.

One of the most challenging and rewarding problems I worked on was during the Rethink Systems Product Management cohort in 2024. In week three, it was my turn to lead the team, and we were tasked with solving problems faced by content creators using generative AI.

At the time, I was 20 years old and relatively new to product management. I suddenly had to lead a team that included individuals with 20+ years of professional experience. The program also had a weekly ranking system, and until then our team had never reached the top three. The pressure to perform was extremely high.

The first day was chaotic. I had no clear idea how to lead the team, structure the work, assign tasks, or define direction. I felt intense pressure and self-doubt, but my teammates were incredibly supportive and trusted me despite my inexperience.

That night, I stayed awake the entire time reflecting and preparing. I studied product frameworks, watched lectures, read material, and tried to absorb everything I could about leadership and product execution within a single day. My brain was operating in a hyper-focused mode.

From the next day onward, we shifted into execution. Our team worked together every night from 9 PM to 2 AM. I reorganized the team into smaller pods and assigned tasks based on people’s interests rather than just their experience. It was a risky decision, but it increased ownership and motivation within the team.

I doubled down on product discovery. We conducted more user interviews, deeper competitor analysis, and extensive root-cause analysis to understand the real problems content creators were facing.

Within seven days, we decided to build and test an MVP. At that time, AI coding tools were not very capable, so we designed a manual but automated workflow for generating YouTube content using generative AI.

The workflow automated the entire content pipeline:

Ideation → Script → Image generation → Video creation → Music and voiceover.

Using this system, we were able to create fully produced YouTube videos in around five minutes.

To validate the idea, we generated and published 14 AI-created YouTube videos in seven days. These videos collectively received over 200,000 views, demonstrating strong early traction. The strategy focused on niche targeting and consistent content production.

For our final presentation, we also decided to take a creative risk. Instead of a standard pitch, we created a short skit to demonstrate the product concept, making the presentation more engaging and memorable.

In the end, our team won first place that week.

For me, the biggest takeaway wasn’t just the result. It was learning how to lead under pressure, learn rapidly, organize a diverse team, and turn an idea into a validated product experiment within a very short timeframe.

Interestingly, one of my teammates later decided to continue building the idea as a full product, which made the experience even more meaningful.

While working on the project, we also noticed that AI would sometimes seem to “get fatigued” and start hallucinating or producing inconsistent results. Because of this, patience became extremely important. Rewriting prompts and experimenting with different instructions was often a hit-or-miss process.

To improve the results, we eventually created a custom GPT and built a dedicated project with a lot of context and training examples to help the model generate more consistent outputs.

Another major issue was text generation within the images. None of the models we used were able to generate clean and consistent text, so we had to add the text manually during the editing process.

Despite all these challenges, we were eventually able to complete and create the comic.

One of the most challenging and impactful problems I have worked on is building MedyVend, a technology-enabled teleconsultation and medicine dispensing system designed to improve access to healthcare in rural and underserved areas.

During my clinical practice and healthcare work, I observed that many patients in smaller towns and villages often travel long distances just to consult a doctor or obtain prescribed medicines. This delay frequently leads to worsening of health conditions and increased financial burden. The challenge was to design a system that could bring both doctor consultation and access to medicines closer to the patient, while maintaining medical safety and compliance.

The idea evolved into MedyVend — a connected device that allows a patient to consult a remote doctor through telemedicine, after which the doctor can remotely dispense the prescribed medicines through the machine. While the concept sounds simple, implementing it required solving multiple technical and operational challenges.

On the technical side, we had to integrate teleconsultation technology, secure connectivity, and a remotely controlled medicine dispensing mechanism that could work reliably even in low-connectivity rural environments. Ensuring the accuracy and safety of medicine dispensing, maintaining audit trails, and building a secure system for doctors to authorize medicine release were key challenges.

On the non-technical side, we had to navigate regulatory considerations, build trust among doctors and pharmacies, and design a sustainable operational model for rural deployment. Convincing stakeholders that a technology-driven solution could safely extend healthcare access required extensive discussions and demonstrations.

Through continuous iteration, partnerships with healthcare institutions, and strong focus on patient safety, we successfully developed and deployed the MedyVend system. The project has helped demonstrate how technology can bridge the healthcare access gap and has opened pathways for scaling telemedicine-enabled healthcare infrastructure in underserved regions.

This experience reinforced my belief that meaningful innovation in healthcare requires not only technology but also deep understanding of clinical workflows, regulatory frameworks, and on-ground realities.

Some of the most urgent crises facing vulnerable communities don't make headlines the way they should. They exist in the margins — in the spaces where systems have failed and people are left to navigate survival alone.
I've been thinking about five of them.
Sex trafficking doesn't begin in the shadows. It begins in the cracks — poverty, instability, a lack of safe options. By the time trafficking is visible, the conditions that made someone vulnerable have usually been present for years. Prevention lives upstream, long before the crisis point.
Caregiving is one of the most essential and most invisible forms of labour in our society. The people who care for our elderly, our sick, our disabled — disproportionately women, disproportionately women of colour — do so with little pay, little protection, and almost no support for their own wellbeing. We have built an entire healthcare economy on their backs and largely pretended not to notice.
Domestic violence is rarely a single event. It is a pattern — of control, of erosion, of someone being slowly convinced that they have no options. The barriers to leaving are practical as much as they are emotional: financial dependence, housing, children, fear of what comes next.
Food deserts are a geography of inequality made edible. When your neighbourhood has three fast food restaurants and no grocery store, your health outcomes are being determined by your zip code, not your choices. Processed food isn't a lifestyle preference for people in these communities — it's often the only option on the shelf.
These crises look different on the surface. Different causes, different faces, different policy conversations. But follow any one of them far enough and you arrive at the same place.
The one problem with many faces is powerlessness — the systematic removal of choice, safety, resource, and dignity from people who were never given enough of any of it to begin with.
Everything else is a symptom.

My hypothesis: people who share Jungian personality types dress similarly. Not identically, but in ways that are patterned and predictable. The introvert who reaches for muted tones and clean lines. The intuitive who layers textures and takes risks. The feeling type who dresses for connection, not status. If Jung could map the architecture of the human psyche, I think that architecture shows up in our wardrobes too — we just haven't measured it yet.
If that correlation holds, the implications get interesting fast.
Imagine an app that starts with a Jungian personality assessment and ends with a fully articulated personal brand — not just "here are colours that suit you" but a deep reflection of who you are and how you naturally want to show up in the world. From there, the content engine writes itself. Physicians are brilliant scientists and, more often than not, accidental leaders.
Medical school teaches you to diagnose disease. Nobody teaches you how to run a room, navigate hierarchy, or build trust with the colleague down the hall whose specialty you were quietly trained to consider less important than your own. In hospital systems, that gap doesn't stay quiet. It shows up in patient care.
One of my most meaningful projects started with a hunch and a survey. I set out to measure something most organisations consider unmeasurable: trust. Not engagement. Not satisfaction. Trust — specifically, how much each physician department trusted the others, and how much the hospital trusted them.
What came back was a map of 12 years of unspoken tension. Twelve departments with significant interdepartmental trust erosion. Seven departments carrying an overall trust score of just 40% — as rated by their own colleagues. The CMO's target was 85%.
I designed a series of cross-departmental workshops to surface the dysfunction, and structured leadership development for the departments furthest from the line. Within a year, every trust score moved. Physician wellbeing scores rose 75%. And patient experience scores — the number that arguably matters most — climbed from 57% to 91%.
It turns out when doctors trust each other, patients feel it.

Weekly Shipping: You should expect to build and ship actual products, such as a RAG app for niche datasets or a tool-using agent that calls external APIs.

FAANG-Standard Capstones: Most high-level cohorts culminate in a capstone project designed to mimic real-world business challenges, which will serve as the centerpiece of your new portfolio.

# The Paw People – Product Builder 1-Pager

## The Mission

> **Healthy, hygienic, and longer lives for pets —  
> delivered to ease up every paw parent's life —  
> while enabling the growth of pet service businesses.**

---

## The Problem

The €3.2B European pet grooming and services market runs on **1990s operations**:

| Pain Point | Impact |
|------------|--------|
| 15–19% of appointments end in no-shows | €18K lost revenue/year per salon |
| Salon owners spend 2+ hours/day on manual bookings | Lost productive time |
| No breed-specific tools for scheduling or care | Wrong time slots, bad experiences |
| Pet health data scattered across apps, paper, WhatsApp | Owners have no single source of truth |
| Groomers, vets, trainers can't see each other's notes | Poor handoffs, repeated mistakes |

**Key insight:** Generic CRMs (Attio, HubSpot) model *company relationships*.  
Nobody models the **pet's life** — breed, behavior, health history, hygiene timeline.

---

## The Solution

**The Paw People = Pet Health & Life Data Platform + CRM + Marketplace**

Three layers working together:

### 1. Pet-Centric CRM (for service providers)
- Breed-specific scheduling (Labrador = 90 min, Dachshund = 45 min)
- Behavioral profiles: anxiety level, grooming notes, bite risk
- Automated SMS reminders → reduces no-shows to <5%
- Lifecycle marketing: rebooking campaigns, birthday rewards, seasonal alerts

### 2. Marketplace (for paw parents)
- Search salons, vets, trainers by **breed expertise** and real-time availability
- Transparent pricing by breed (€40–80 depending on coat complexity)
- Reviews filtered by same breed owners ("5 stars from other Labrador owners")
- One-tap rebooking from grooming history

### 3. Pet Health Timeline (the moat)
- Longitudinal record: every grooming visit, vet note, weight change, behavioral flag
- Simple **Wellness Score** (0–100) updated after each service visit
- Paw parent gets: *"Bella's coat is trending worse — book a bath this week"*
- Provider gets: *"3 Labradors overdue for grooming, 2 with rising anxiety scores"*

The most challenging project I've worked on is building Vyomera as a solo founder with no institutional backing. The core problem I tackled is that GCC banking infrastructure has no open banking standard meaning there's no official API to pull a user's financial data across banks like ENBD, ADCB, or FAB. This created both a technical and a regulatory hurdle: how do you build a meaningful personal finance product when you can't programmatically access user data?

Technical hurdles: I built a working prototype using Google AI Studio and Streamlit where users upload their bank statements (PDFs), and a generative AI pipeline parses, classifies, and analyzes their spending, debt load, and credit utilization — returning 5–7 GCC-specific actionable insights within seconds. Building an accurate PDF parsing + RAG pipeline that handles Arabic/English bank statement formats across multiple UAE institutions required significant prompt engineering and iteration.

Non-technical hurdles: As a solo founder, I had to simultaneously build the product, create the pitch narrative, model the business financials, design the go-to-market, and engage investors — all without a co-founder to split the load. I prepared and submitted a Y Combinator application and had a live investor call with Beco Capital (a $820M+ AUM Dubai-based VC) while still in prototype stage, which forced me to develop extreme clarity on the business model and market sizing under real pressure.

How I succeeded: I reframed the product from a consumer subscription app to a B2B2C embedded finance distribution channel — essentially positioning Vyomera as replacing bank DSA networks and performance marketing spend, which gave us a clear enterprise revenue model without needing millions of retail subscribers upfront. This pivot sharpened the pitch, made unit economics credible (AED 500+ per financial product conversion × volume), and gave institutional investors a familiar monetization lens to evaluate the business.
